title: The as const Assertion knowledge check

questions.prompt: What does a TypeScript type assertion do?
options: It guarantees the asserted type is correct.
It tells the compiler to treat an expression as a type; it does not validate the value at runtime.
It inserts a runtime validator for every field.
It changes the JavaScript value into a different object.
questions.answer_key: It tells the compiler to treat an expression as a type; it does not validate the value at runtime.
questions.explanation: Use an assertion only when independent evidence justifies it; validation is separate.

questions.prompt: Which statement is correct about “The as const Assertion”?
options: The concept should be demonstrated with readonly literal inference and checked against its intended contract.
The safest approach is to skip diagnostics and trust the first output.
A type assertion automatically validates every value at runtime.
The learner should publish hidden solutions so the exercise can grade itself.
questions.answer_key: The concept should be demonstrated with readonly literal inference and checked against its intended contract.
questions.explanation: The supplied syllabus explicitly includes “Readonly literal inference”; connect it to a concrete example and verify the behavior relevant to this lesson.

questions.prompt: What is a good verification step after practicing “The as const Assertion”?
options: Assume const assertions for configuration objects is unnecessary because the code has type annotations.
Ignore compiler or test failures if the interface looks correct.
Treat passing a static token check as proof that the program executed correctly.
Check preserving literal types, include a meaningful failure case where appropriate, and document any runtime or version assumptions.
questions.answer_key: Check preserving literal types, include a meaningful failure case where appropriate, and document any runtime or version assumptions.
questions.explanation: The syllabus includes “Preserving literal types”. Verification should match the concept: type-level checks, runtime tests, configuration checks or human review as appropriate.
